note: Track styles (theory-progressions), step 4: the changes of a jazz standard as a major ii–V–I chained to the ii–V–i of the relative minor, the turnaround, then the same changes in other keys.

exercise.title: Jazz standards: ii–V–Is in a chain
exercise.why: A jazz standard is mostly ii–V–Is joined end to end, in the major key and in its relative minor, so spotting a ii–V tells you which home chord comes next.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing track, in swing. Bars 1 to 3 are a ii–V–I in G major, bar 4 is the 4th chord, and bars 5 to 7 are a ii–V–i in E minor, the relative minor.
Call out "major" or "minor" each time the backing track lands on a home chord.
Once you hear each landing coming a bar early, look away from the chord boxes and call them again.

Press Play below to start the backing track: four chords that end a chorus and lead back to its top. The last two are a ii and a V, so the home chord at the top of the next round is the I they point to.
Call out 1, 6, 2 or 5 on each change until the numbers come without looking.

Press Play below to start the backing track: the eight bars of the first block again. Look away from the chord boxes and call out "major" or "minor" on each home chord.
Once both landings are easy to hear, listen in another key. Use the Key selector below to change the key, then press Play to start the backing track again.
When you change the key, the chords are new but the chain is the same: a ii–V–I in major, then a ii–V–i in its relative minor.
